chapter: Brown's Band in Chicago and New York
title: How the band was hired for Chicago
summary: A dancer's manager heard the band on a wagon and Lopez arranged the trip; the lineup and Raymond Lopez as boss.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: Down the back. Uh, then, uh, what happened when you all left for Chicago? How'd the whole business start as far as you remember?

Well, I'm positive on that because, uh, you see, we were playing on a tailgate, on a wagon. And, uh, a fella named, uh, a fella named Joe Gorham, uh, a woman dancer by the name of Myrtle Howard. And she was appearing at West End. At that time, they had a theater out there. Yeah. And she was a big-time act. So this fella asked us if we'd consider going to Chicago. Well, he just heard you the one time on the wagon? That's all. He only heard about two tunes and that was it. Uh-huh. He, we were sold. So, he made an appointment. And, uh, he was a big-time actor. Uh, he was a big-time actor.
Uh, he was a big-time actor. Uh, he was a big-time actor.

Uh, he was a big-time actor. Uh, he was a big-time actor. Uh, he was a big-time actor. Uh, he was a big-time actor. He, we were sold. So, he made an appointment. And instead of Tommy Brown going to see Myrtle Howard, who was staying at the Old Groomall Hotel, Raymond Lopez and I went to see her. Raymond did the talking. And we were, uh, ordered the job right away. In the meantime, Joe Gorham had got in touch with Smiley Carbett and told him where to find the air. And so, Carbett says, All right. And said, send the transportation. Well, he sent the transportation. And that time, it took us 29 hours to ride it. Uh-huh. I think it was 1850 round trip.
Was that called the Panama Limited then, still? No.

No, I don't remember it being called the Panama Limited at that time. They, uh, they had one good train. But, uh, I think that was an extra fare train. I think, I'm pretty sure the fare was 1850 round trip.
Well, who, uh, then when you all spoke to, uh, the lady, what's her name? Oh, Myrtle Howard?
Yeah. And she, uh, you all made arrangements with her at the...
Oh, yeah. Yeah. You gonna back her up or what? No, no. No, no.
No, no. No, no. We were to go up there as a band. I know.
This was an attraction. Not with her act.

No, no. No, no. No, she had two good bookings to fool around with us. She, she didn't want anything like that. Uh, she was a, she was a big, big, big, big Vortigil star. Mm-hmm. She was appearing here. But, uh, she was instrumental through her manager, Gorham, getting us up to Chicago. Mm-hmm. And when we went to Chicago, we... Wait a minute, now, who, who was the whole band? Well, it was, uh, Lopez on trumpet, Gus Miller on clarinet, Tommy Brown on trombone, I was playing piano, and Bill Lambert on drums. There's no bass. Mm-hmm. So we went at five.
Uh-huh. Well, now, uh, was, it went under the name of Brown's Band?
But they didn't call it Brown's Band from Dixieland then at that time?
No, no, no. They, uh, they, we left here with Raymond Lopez. Uh-huh. Not Tommy Brown. Raymond was the boss. Raymond was the boss.
That's right. Uh-huh. Raymond was the boss.
